record.paper_title: Crystal Nucleation in Liquids: Open Questions and Future Challenges in Molecular Dynamics Simulations
record.original_question: Can classical nucleation theory be improved into a universal theoretical framework for crystal nucleation in liquids, or do the system-specific behaviors of different supercooled liquids mean that progress will require different ad hoc variants of classical nucleation theory and different tailored enhanced-sampling methods for different classes of systems and conditions?

evidence.quote: Thus, we believe that any sort of theoretical universal approach, a brand new CNT, so to say, will be unlikely to significantly further the field. Indeed we fear that the same reasoning will hold for the computational methods required. We cannot think of a single enhanced sampling technique capable of tackling the complexity of crystal nucleation as a whole.
Whether CNT can be effectively improved in a universal fashion is unclear.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Classical nucleation theory (CNT) models the rate of formation of a new crystalline phase from a metastable supercooled liquid by treating an emerging nucleus of the stable phase as a spherical cluster whose free energy of formation is written as the sum of a negative bulk term proportional to its volume (driven by the chemical potential difference Δμ between liquid and solid) and a positive surface term proportional to its area (controlled by an effective liquid–solid interfacial tension γ). The resulting free-energy barrier ΔG* = 16πγ³/(3 ρ_s² Δμ²) and an attempt/attachment kinetic prefactor together yield a predicted nucleation rate J = J₀ exp(−ΔG*/k_B T).

Different classes of supercooled liquids (e.g., simple atomic Lennard-Jones-like fluids, hard spheres, network-forming liquids such as water and silica, metallic glass-formers, colloidal suspensions, and molecular crystals with polymorphism) display markedly different nucleation behavior, including non-spherical or polymorph-mixed nuclei, two-step nucleation through precursor phases, strongly curvature- and temperature-dependent interfacial tensions, and non-classical attachment kinetics.

Question: Does there exist a single, universally valid extension of classical nucleation theory — i.e., a closed analytical framework, derivable from generic statistical-mechanical assumptions about a metastable liquid, that predicts crystal nucleation rates and pathways quantitatively across all such classes of supercooled liquids and thermodynamic conditions — or is it provably necessary that any quantitatively predictive theory must be replaced by system-specific (ad hoc) modifications of CNT, paired with different tailored enhanced-sampling computational methods, depending on the class of system and the regime of supercooling considered?
artifact.status_search_result: The question of whether CNT can be unified into a universal predictive framework for crystal nucleation across all supercooled liquids remains an open conceptual and modeling challenge. Reviews and recent works on nucleation continue to report system-specific corrections (curvature-dependent surface tension, two-step nucleation, non-classical pathways) without a single accepted universal generalization, and no proof of impossibility exists either.

status_evidence.title: Crystal nucleation in liquids: Open questions and future challenges
status_evidence.snippet: Whether CNT can be effectively improved in a universal fashion is unclear; we fear no single enhanced sampling technique can tackle the complexity of crystal nucleation as a whole.
status_evidence.claim: The universality of an improved CNT framework is explicitly stated as unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Recent advances in classical and non-classical nucleation theories
status_evidence.snippet: Many recent studies refine CNT with system-specific corrections (curvature-dependent γ, two-step pathways) but no universal predictive theory has been established.
status_evidence.claim: Current literature continues to use ad hoc, system-specific extensions of CNT rather than a unified theory.
